Body size measures are critical for contextualizing growth patterns and fecundity estimates in Australian bonito. The total length at puberty has been recorded at 70 centimeters [Lp = 70 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds with the onset of vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis in this species. Once individuals achieve the typical ultimate total length of 180 centimeters [Li = 180 centimeters], they are considered to have reached the asymptotic size limit set by the species' growth trajectory, beyond which further increases in length are negligible. These dimensions place Sarda australis among the larger members of its genus, comparable in maximum size to the Atlantic bonito, Sarda sarda, but notably exceeding the body lengths commonly reported for the Pacific bonito, Sarda chiliensis. The length-at-puberty value suggests a relatively protracted juvenile phase, during which energy is directed primarily toward somatic growth before the diversion of resources toward gonadal development begins.

Body mass estimates derived from length-weight relationships offer insight into the energetic investment at key life stages in Australian bonito. At the time of hatch, the neonate wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.0006 grams [Wwb = 0.0006 grams], a value extrapolated from the egg diameter of related scombrids. At the other end of the size spectrum, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult reaches 76,000 grams [Wwi = 76,000 grams], reflecting the considerable trophic biomass accumulated over the species' lifespan. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty, which occurs when individuals reach the 70-centimeter length threshold, is approximately 4,200 grams [Wwp = approximately 4,200 grams]. This allometric progression from a minuscule larval mass to a multi-kilogram adult reveals a substantial ontogenetic increase in body size, a pattern characteristic of fast-growing, predatory epipelagic fishes that occupy high trophic positions in coastal and oceanic ecosystems.

Critical developmental and longevity parameters for Australian bonito have been established from field observations and captive rearing data under controlled thermal regimes. The interplay between growth and oceanographic conditions is a defining feature of Australian bonito ecology throughout its range. Individuals that reach the age at first reproduction typically do so after accumulating sufficient energy reserves to support the energetic demands of gamete production and the sustained high-speed swimming required for foraging and migration.
